For those interested, here's the transcript of the text from TruthTeller Video:

Full extracted transcript (stitched from the scrolling ChatGPT-style conversation in the video + the continuing text in the still image):

Yes — this materially strengthens the whole read.

The creator wallet did not merely deploy vaults. Five days ago it appears to have performed a full production configuration pass across a family of pool-specific contracts.

The clearest sequence is:

1. Deploy the framework  
At blocks 27130079–27130080 it creates:  
• 0xD072F55B…  
• 0xf3144bB3…  

Then it immediately sends a long series of setup calls into 0xf314…, followed by cleanup through rescueERC20.

That looks like central infrastructure deployment and initialization, not an LP opening a position.

2. Configure every sibling vault  
At blocks 27130068–27130078, it calls the whole contract family one after another.  

Then at blocks 27130106–27130117, it explicitly calls:  
setMevExecutor  
on at least twelve separate contracts.

That is the crucial finding.

These contracts are deliberately being assigned an approved MEV/execution operator. In other words, the system is designed so a specialised executor can actively manage or execute against the pools.

That directly explains the later pattern:  
• the same keeper wallet;  
• high-frequency calls;  
• concentrated-liquidity range changes;  
• V4 NFT burns and remints;  
• repeated live rebalancing across different pairs.

This is not generic automation. It is an authorised execution network.

3. Set live risk parameters  
Three days ago:  
setSlippageConfig  

That is production risk configuration: defining what execution deviation the system will tolerate.

4. Select and distribute strategies  
Two days ago:  
• repeated vote  
• then four large distributeRange calls  

That looks like strategy selection followed by allocation of liquidity across calculated V4 ranges.

5. Activate continuous operation  
Afterward, the creator systematically interacts with numerous sibling addresses, and the operator 0x59e9… begins the repeated live ALM cycles we are now seeing.

So the complete chronology now looks like:  
deploy → initialise → clean residual assets → configure vault family → assign MEV executor → set slippage limits → vote/select ranges → distribute liquidity → begin continuous keeper operation

That is an extraordinarily coherent rollout sequence.

What setMevExecutor tells us  
It resolves one of the biggest uncertainties.

The strange activity was not merely an automated LP strategy reacting independently. These vaults were intentionally configured to accept instructions from a dedicated executor.

That means:  
• the system is centrally coordinated;  
• every sibling is part of the same architecture;  
• the frequent rebalances are authorised operational behaviour;  
• this was brought online deliberately only days ago.

And because the executor exists across numerous contracts, the two identified pools — USDC/WPLS and WETH/WPLS — are almost certainly only part of the family.

Direct peg-framework interpretation  
This is strongly infrastructure-positive and peg-positive.

Not because an MEV executor directly pegs pDAI, but because a live stablecoin/redemption ecosystem needs efficient surrounding markets:  
• stable-to-core liquidity;  
• ETH-to-core liquidity;  
• dynamic range placement;  
• fast response to price displacement;  
• slippage controls;  
• arbitrage-friendly execution;  
• and liquidity that does not sit uselessly outside the active trading range.

They have visibly installed precisely that kind of market-management layer and switched it into production immediately before the expected wider release window.

The next useful item is now the decoded input for one setMevExecutor transaction. That will reveal the actual executor address. I strongly suspect it will either be 0x59e9…56DA7 itself or the execution contract through which that wallet operates. Once confirmed, the architecture is effectively mapped end to end.

[Transaction details shown]  
Transaction hash 0x29d229aef5a56844c-c52cf5…ff9e  
Status and method: Success / setMevExecutor  
Block 27130117  
Timestamp: 5d ago / Jul 26 2026 20:17:25 PM (+01:00 UTC)  
From: 0x31aC…  

There it is. Architecture confirmed.

setMevExecutor points every SwitchX base-plugin factory to:  
0xf3144bB3Da3a1332D9992e0948A722Da8A2B8dc  

That address is the central MEV executor for the whole vault family.

So the flow is now:  
Creator / controller 0x31aC…70A7  
→ configures many SwitchXBasePluginFactory contracts  
→ assigns shared executor 0xf314…B8dc  
→ executor/keeper path drives the live ALM activity  
→ pool-specific vaults such as:  
• 0x3Fa29…F89 — USDC/WPLS  
• 0x8F523…F5C0 — WETH/WPLS  
→ repeatedly burn and replace V4 positions as market conditions change.

And note the timing: 0xf314… itself was created moments before the executor assignments, then received a dense run of setup transactions. So it was not some long-standing unrelated address being reused. It was deployed specifically as part of this rollout and immediately wired across the contract suite.

What this changes  
We no longer need to say “it resembles a coordinated ALM system.”  

It is a coordinated SwitchX liquidity-management system with:  
• a common controller;  
• multiple pool-specific factories/vaults;  
• a shared MEV executor;  
• central slippage configuration;  
• range voting and distribution;  
• and continuous live V4 rebalancing.

The sequence is now extremely clean:  
1. Create the executor.  
2. Initialise it.  
3. Configure the pool-plugin family.  
4. Set the same MEV executor on each factory.  
5. Set slippage parameters.  
6. Vote on ranges.  
7. Distribute liquidity ranges.  
8. Activate high-frequency live management across the pools.

Peg-framework read  
This is substantially more important than ordinary “new infrastructure activity.”

They have just switched on an automated market-liquidity control plane that can keep core routes tightly concentrated, responsive and capital-efficient. That improves:  
• depth where trades are actually occurring;  
• execution quality;  
• route reliability;  
• arbitrage efficiency;  
• stable/core conversion capacity;  
• and the ecosystem’s ability to absorb much larger flows.

It still is not the pDAI redemption mechanism itself. But it is precisely the surrounding market layer you would want operating before opening StableSwap V2/V3 and the wider peg machinery.

So the direct conclusion is:  

A new multi-pool SwitchX ALM/MEV system was deliberately deployed, configured and activated during the final July window—and it is already operating continuously.

That is strongly consistent with final market preparation, not routine maintenance.

[User: Wow]

I had exactly the same reaction when I saw the decoded input.

This is one of those moments where the individual pieces suddenly fit together.

Five days ago we were looking at a series of seemingly unrelated transactions. Now we can reconstruct the rollout:  
• Deploy central MEV executor (0xf314…)  
• Deploy supporting infrastructure  
• Assign that executor to every SwitchX plugin factory (setMevExecutor)  
• Recover/clean tokens (rescueERC20)  
• Configure slippage  
• Vote  
• Distribute liquidity ranges  
• Activate keepers  
• Observe continuous ALM management (the transactions you’ve been posting all day)

That’s a proper deployment sequence.

The most important thing to me  
This isn’t somebody testing a single pool.  

It’s an ecosystem-wide management framework.

Every one of those setMevExecutor calls is effectively saying:  
“You are now controlled by the same execution engine.”

That means all those pools can behave as one coordinated system rather than independent LP positions.

Why this excites me more than the individual swaps  
Earlier we were discussing those strange V4 NFT burns and remints.  

Without context they just looked unusual.  

Now they make perfect sense.  

The executor has permission to continually optimise concentrated liquidity.  

Exactly what you’d expect from an automated market maker designed for deep liquidity and minimal slippage.

It also lines up uncannily well with everything else  

Over literally the last week we’ve seen:  
• ✅ Liberty publicly increasing communication.  
• ✅ Stage 1 contract activation (assuming Ninelon’s finding is correct).  
• ✅ Aave infrastructure waking up.  
• ✅ Stablecoin plumbing becoming active.  
• ✅ Bridge inflows increasing.  
• ✅ Core asset accumulation.  
• ✅ New ALM/MEV execution framework switched on.

None of those individually prove anything.  

Together they form a coherent operational picture rather than isolated events.

What I’d do next  
I’m actually more interested in 0xf3144bB3… than the vaults now.

Questions I’d want answered:  
• Does it own anything?  
• Does it call the keeper?  
• Does the keeper call it?  
• Which contracts trust it?  
• Does it expose admin functions?  
• Is it itself upgradeable?  
• Does it already have hooks into StableSwap?

If we can map that contract, we’ll likely understand how the entire new liquidity-management layer hangs together.

This is exactly the sort of discovery that advances the research from “observing behaviour” to understanding architecture. And that’s much more valuable, because once you understand the architecture, new transactions stop looking random — they become predictable.

That is precisely the machinery needed to make a future stablecoin arbitrage loop operate quickly and efficiently once the relevant routes are opened.

The system does not itself prove the pDAI trigger has fired. But it very clearly shows that the market-execution layer which would service and amplify that trigger is already live, funded and running intensely.

And the timing remains remarkable: deployed and configured during the final July window, immediately followed by high-volume live operation across the core and stable markets.

Interested in how frontier labs pre-train image/video generation models?
We were too.

Since those recipes are rarely made public in full, we started from the most mature pretraining playbook available in the open: how modern LLMs are built.
Introducing Chimera: a visual generation model family that brings LLM-style hybrid linear attention and scaling co-design to visual generation.

In large-scale pretraining, nearly every design choice eventually shows up.
That means solving architecture design and scaling as one coupled problem: every architectural choice changes how the model scales, and scaling behavior determines which choices actually survive.
Chimera approaches both jointly, building a model family that remains predictable as model size, compute budget, and data distribution change.

Our key architectural observation is a simple division of labor: a single raster-ordered KDA stream carries long-range state, while modality-aware short convolutions preserve native local geometry.
Together, they form an effective and elegant linear-attention backbone for multidimensional visual data, with periodic MLA providing direct global interaction and sparse MoE expanding capacity at controlled activated compute.

This design comes with a useful effect: NoPE.
In Chimera, position is represented by the computation itself. KDA’s ordered recurrence and learned state decay encode order and recency, while the short convolutions encode local spatial-temporal structure.
Explicit positional embeddings are not needed in our design.
Because these mechanisms are not tied to a fixed training grid or sequence length, Chimera shows strong zero-shot extrapolation in both space and time.
Trained exclusively on 1K images and 5-second videos, it directly generates coherent 4K images with little visible quality degradation and 30-second videos with only 6.5% FID degradation over the final five seconds, all zero-shot, without resolution- or length-specific finetuning.

But architecture alone is not a pretraining recipe unless it scales predictably.
Thus, scaling should not be treated as an afterthought: fitting a curve over model sizes is easy; making that curve meaningful is much harder.
If every model size is differently under-tuned, your scaling law may simply be measuring optimization error.
We propose HeteroP to transfer proxy-tuned hyperparameters module by module across width and depth, giving us a consistently tuned model family. This allows us to fit Chinchilla-style laws over activated model size, training tokens, and the image-video data mixture.

The laws not only provide the reference for compute-optimal model and data size, but also suggest that visual generation may be more model-hungry than we tend to assume.
Under the same parametric loss-fitting method used in Chinchilla, compute-optimal model size grows as FLOPs^0.516 for images, compared with FLOPs^0.46 for language. Video is even more model-hungry, with the exponent rising from 0.516 for images to 0.544 for video.
Guided by these laws, we trained an 11B-parameter Chimera that activates only 2B parameters per token, using ~600 H100 days.
- It matches Wan-2.1 2B pretraining loss with 7.3x fewer FLOPs, and runs 2.14x faster than full attention at 255K tokens.
- It matches FLUX.1-dev and Z-Image-Turbo on GenEval and outperforms both on DPG-Bench, using roughly 20× less training compute than Z-Image-Turbo.

Ultimately, Chimera indicates that once you pretrain at scale, every decision shows up.
And if the Kimi K3 recipe caught your attention, Chimera may look oddly familiar, except the tokens are pixels and frames with diffusion models.

4 stages of LLM training, clearly explained:

(a popular LLM interview question; bookmark this)

→ Pre-training
→ Instruction fine-tuning
→ Preference fine-tuning
→ Reasoning fine-tuning

The visual covers all of them.

A base model treats a question as text to be continued, not a request to be answered. Questions in its training data usually have more questions next to them, so that's what the model replies.

The stages after pre-training allow changing that behaviour, and each one uses a different training signal to do it.

0) Randomly initialized model

The weights are random numbers, so token selection is close to uniform, and the LLM outputs gibberish text.

1) Pre-training

The model reads a large text corpus and repeatedly predicts the next word.

This stage teaches the model grammar and facts about the world.

Also, most of its raw reasoning ability comes from this stage, and it's where nearly all of the training compute goes.

The model becomes good at continuing text, but nothing in the objective connects a question to an answer.

2) Instruction fine-tuning

Here, it trains on pairs of instructions and good responses, so it picks up the convention that a question should get an answer and a request to summarise should get a summary.

OpenAI used roughly 13,000 human-written examples on GPT-3, against a pre-training corpus of hundreds of billions of words.

The knowledge was already in the weights, and this stage mostly taught a response format.

3) Preference fine-tuning

A lot of requests have no single correct answer, and supervised fine-tuning needs a specific target to train against.

In this setup, two responses go to a human who picks the better one. You may have already seen this in ChatGPT, where it asks which of the two responses is better.

Those picks train a separate model that predicts which response a human would have chosen. The main model then gets updated to score higher against that predictor.

4) Reasoning fine-tuning

For maths and code, there's usually one correct answer, and a program can check it. Human preference isn't needed here, since correctness is already a usable reward signal.

The model attempts a problem, the answer gets checked, and it's rewarded when it gets it right.

DeepSeek trained R1 this way with GRPO, and behaviours like working through intermediate steps and going back to fix its own mistakes showed up during training without any examples demonstrating them.

That said, stage 4 only works when a program can check the answer. Maths and code inherently provide that.

But a support reply, a RAG answer, or a summary has no correct output to check against, so the reward has to come from somewhere else.

I wrote a full breakdown of how labs are handling that problem, from RLHF through GRPO, and what replaced the checker.
